titleSource: Cautions and Comparisons: How to Burn $1,000,000 a Night

sittings.bodyEn: The New Rich spend time and mobility on a life that is already underway. Deferrers store the good life for a finish line that can arrive after the years that needed it. People usually want the experiences they believe only a fortune can buy, so the aim is that freedom, and a large balance is one route toward it. Options, the ability to choose, are the power this book is building. A chase for more cash, with no picture of the life, is the wrong train, because the trophies can cost decades beside people you dislike. This chapter separates the two groups by their goals, since a small change in the goal changes the work.

terms.hook: People who buy time and mobility now, and spend both on a life already in motion.
People who save the good life for a finish line at the end of work.

sittings.bodyEn: Read the pairs in order, because a wording change rewrites the work, and the first pair applies to employees too. Deferrers want to work for themselves. The New Rich want other people doing the work. Deferrers want to work whenever the mood arrives. The New Rich want to stop work that exists only to fill the day. They keep the smallest load that still produces the largest effect, which this chapter calls the minimum effective load. Inactivity is not their picture of a good month, because the point of the free time is doing what excites you.

terms.hook: The least work that still produces the largest effect.

sittings.bodyEn: Deferrers want to retire early. The New Rich spread recovery and adventure through life as mini-retirements, and they treat excitement as the use of that time. Deferrers want to be the boss. The New Rich want to be the owner, with someone else keeping the trains on time. Deferrers aim at a pile of purchases and one distant payday, such as a sale of the company or a retirement pot. The New Rich aim at doing and becoming, with tools only as means, money arriving every day, and a large payday second. They want more quality and less clutter, plus reserves, and they refuse to spend weeks haggling for objects that never give the life a purpose.

terms.hook: Recovery or adventure placed through life, on a repeating schedule.
The person who owns the system, while someone else keeps it running.

sittings.bodyEn: Deferrers want freedom from tasks they dislike. The New Rich want that freedom and the resolve to chase dreams without sliding back into work for its own sake. Years of repetition can bury hobbies, so you may have to dig the old ones back up and name new ones. Clearing only the disliked work leaves an empty week. That empty week is a vacuum. The goal is to fill it by pursuing the best experiences you can name, not by collecting a second pile of tasks.

terms.hook: Activity kept alive because the day looks wrong when it is empty.

sittings.bodyEn: The practical power of money depends on four levers: the work itself, the hour, the place, and the people beside you. This chapter calls that bundle the freedom multiplier. An eighty-hour week at five hundred thousand dollars a year can leave less power than a quarter of those hours at forty thousand dollars, when the smaller income includes freedom of when, where, and how you live. Price the life each pile of money actually buys, and the larger salary can be the weaker one. Freeing time and place can make the same money worth several times as much. Exchange rates are not the reason. Being financially rich and being able to live like a millionaire are two different facts.

terms.hook: Money becomes more useful as you control what, when, where, and with whom.

sittings.bodyEn: The opening scene is a warning, not a fantasy to copy. A man rich enough to lose enormous sums on a weekend trip liked none of the businesses that paid for it. He had spent more than thirty years with people he did not like, buying things he did not need, and the prizes had become the schedule. That ending is the one this chapter tells you to refuse. The same pages say a serious version of living well, including travel that looks expensive, can cost less than familiar rent once time and place are free. Count the life the money produces, then decide which of the two goals you are actually serving.

One portrait is an employee who rearranges the week, reaches about ninety percent of the results in a tenth of the time, and uses the rest for family travel. Another is an owner who drops the least profitable customers and projects, hands the operation to other people, and travels while a remote site shows her own illustration work. A third is a student whose small video-rental niche brings in about five thousand dollars a month for roughly two hours a week, beside a full-time cause he cares about. The lives do not match. Each one starts by replacing an assumption about how work has to look. Joining the group means learning this vocabulary and throwing out a borrowed definition of success.

A young skier kept the company he had started with his brother and still reached an Olympic podium, by moving to a smaller and more flexible team. The coaches wanted more hours on the hill. The results were already there, and the tight part was the menu of choices in front of him. A family sailed about fifteen thousand miles in roughly fifteen months for about eighteen or nineteen thousand dollars, less than ordinary rent and bread at home. Hundreds of families leave that same country each year for a version of the trip. The crossing had waited behind a growing list of reasons, until one of them saw that the reasons would only multiply. Children had been the reason to postpone, and then the reason the trip was worth taking, because the boat forced patience and made books more interesting than a wall of water.

After the crossing, that family was already planning a mountain base and a small workshop to fund more travel. One completed trip created the appetite for the next. Another account uses a mini-retirement so a parent and child can live at a forest school instead of hauling the child back to a desk across town. The pattern matches the three portraits. Replace the assumption that the menu in front of you is the full menu. Then spend the freed time on a life you can describe. There is almost always a side door when the presented choice is this or that.

The New Rich measure wealth by time and mobility used now. Deferrers save the lifestyle for a later finish line. A job title, a larger pile of purchases, or a single distant payday does not put someone in the first group. The freedom multiplier raises the practical value of money when you control what, when, where, and with whom. Doing half the old work can still produce more money, because the cut removes the half that was filling the day. The first move in every portrait is the same: replace the assumption, then aim the hours at a life you can name.
sittings.prompt: What do the New Rich treat as real wealth in this chapter?
choices: A retirement fund large enough to stop working
Time and mobility, used now on a life they can describe
The title of boss, with more people reporting to them
Trophy purchases that prove the money is real
